text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Add a "safe change" auto-apply layer that runs before any human review. It will catch and fix trivial but common errors like typos, formatting, or missing imports without slowing anyone down. The trade-off is accepting a small risk of false positives—it might tweak something harmless—but the time saved and consistency gained outweigh it.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t just false positives—it’s that "trivial" errors often mask deeper issues. A typo might hide a logic flaw; missing imports could signal a broken dependency. The safer alternative is a pre-review lint pass that flags but doesn’t auto-fix, letting humans judge trade-offs. Settle it by testing the lint pass on 10 recent PRs and measuring how often it catches real vs. trivial issues.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do it. Auto-apply safe fixes before human review—typos, formatting, missing imports—because the time saved outweighs the risk. The trade-off is accepting a small chance of false positives; we’ll log every change so humans can audit and override.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk is that auto-applying fixes before human review creates a blind spot, where subtle but critical issues are inadvertently "fixed" and then overlooked. A better alternative is to implement a hybrid approach, where the pre-review lint pass not only flags potential issues but also provides a confidence score for each fix, allowing humans to review and prioritize accordingly. This would settle the argument by balancing efficiency with the need for human oversight and judgment.

name: Ratchet
text:
DECISION: Auto-apply only *mechanical* fixes (typos, formatting, missing imports) before human review, with full change logs for audit—reject deeper "fixes" that risk masking logic flaws.

Result: A lightweight pre-review layer that saves time without hiding real issues. Owner: Sprocket.
